claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 is in an as-processed hierarchical-heterostructured state featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The stated hierarchical state is produced by arc melting, homogenization, cold rolling, recrystallization, and aging.
The proposed surrogate combines experimentally extracted microstructural descriptors with phase-field damage features.
Variance in atomic planar density, ionization energy, and elastic moduli can serve as descriptors of alloy heterogeneity.
Phase-field damage simulations can represent deformation, material softening, and fracture evolution in a heterogeneous microstructure.
The hybrid surrogate can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The hybrid surrogate will have lower computational cost than conventional CALPHAD and first-principles approaches.
The hybrid surrogate will be more accurate than conventional CALPHAD, first-principles, and standalone machine-learning approaches.
The intended prediction domain is quasi-static uniaxial tensile and fracture testing at room temperature.
Predictions are intended to apply only when composition and hierarchical microstructure remain within the training domain.
Local variations in stiffness and bonding alter stress localization and damage initiation.
Combining heterogeneity descriptors with phase-field outputs improves sensitivity to localized deformation and failure processes.
The model will reduce prediction errors for Young's modulus and yield strength by approximately 30% relative to baseline methods.
The resulting error margins for Young's modulus and yield strength will be approximately 10%.
The model will provide more reliable fracture-toughness predictions than the baseline methods.
The model will be approximately ten times more computationally efficient than the baseline methods.
Existing CALPHAD, first-principles, and standalone machine-learning methods require extensive computation and have difficulty predicting fracture toughness.
Reliability will decline for substantially altered microstructures, out-of-range variance descriptors, high strain rates, or elevated temperatures.
The quantitative accuracy and efficiency gains depend on dataset quality, descriptor extraction, and reproducibility of the hierarchical structure.

The hypothesis is to be falsified if blinded testing fails to show a 30% error reduction for Young's modulus and yield strength, or if fewer than 80% of specimens have toughness predictions within acceptable limits.
